newsitem.title: CANADA: Mobil Canada does not see forming new trusts.
newsitem.headline: Mobil Canada does not see forming new trusts.

text.p: Mobil Corp unit Mobil Oil Canada does not envision setting up another royalty trust with its remaining western Canadian oil and gas assets, despite quick corporate gains after last spring's issue, a Mobil Canada executive said this week.

"A lot of the assets that we sold into the trust were really a distraction to us -- they were taking up some scarce resources of capital, and technical and accounting manpower," Wayne Kubasek, Mobil Canada's vice-president of new business devlopment, said in an interview. "This provided us with an opportunity to move a whole bunch of assets at one time."
But the said the the company was not ruling out moving more assets into an existing trust in the future.
Mobil Canada said in May it was moving more than C$200 million of its oil and gas properties into a royalty trust that is now managed by Calgary-based ARC Financial Corp.
It was among a flurry of similar deals announced over the past year that pay investors regular payouts from the cash flow of energy and mining assets.
Canadian retail investors, faced with low interest rates that made fixed-income securities unattractive, flocked to the new issues, which are also favorable from a tax standpoint.

Other major issues over the past year have included two trusts based on Syncrude Canada Ltd synthetic oil production set up by Gulf Canada Resources Ltd and PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd, the creation of EnerMark Income Fund from Mark Resources assets, a trust formed from Alberta's Luscar coal mining operation and another from output from Iron Ore Co of Canada, set up by Norcen Energy Resources Ltd.
"The question comes down to, are you satisfied with the four percent return on fixed-income or are you willing to go toward nine, 10 percent and above that on some other product?" Kubasek said.
Risks in the publicly traded units are different for investors. In energy trusts, payouts continue only as long as the production from the reserves continues.

Kubasek said the benefit for Mobil in selling its assets into the trust was that the company could devote its resources to key western Canada geographic and strategic areas identified as set for growth.
The popularity of trust units after last year's rush and a brief hiatus this summer, could pick up again if interest rates stay low, he said.

"I think there are properties available in the industry yet," Kubasek said. "It's going to depend on the drivers of the industry itself as to whether they see it as a way to monitize their value in the assets."
